topic: Osteoarthritis: pathophysiology, risk factors, radiographic grading, pharmacological management
synopsis: This JAMA review of hip and knee osteoarthritis separates clinical diagnosis from radiographs and then describes both. Older age and female sex are risk factors for hip and for knee OA. Congenital or acquired anatomic abnormalities, such as hip dysplasia, are additional risk factors for hip OA. African Americans and white people have similar hip-OA prevalence after accounting for race, sex, and body mass index, whereas African Americans, especially women, have a higher prevalence of knee OA. For research grading, Kellgren-Lawrence grade 0 is no pathologic findings, grade 1 questionable osteophytes, grade 2 definite osteophytes, grade 3 definite joint-space narrowing, and grade 4 advanced joint-space narrowing. NSAIDs are called first-line pharmacologic treatment, with a moderate effect versus placebo (standardized mean difference about 0.33). Topical NSAIDs generally have less gastrointestinal toxicity than oral NSAIDs but are less useful for the hip because the joint is recessed. The review also notes that knee OA after an anterior cruciate ligament tear may be mechanistically distinct from obesity-associated OA.
